name: Testosterone-boosting diet (eggs, oysters, red meat)
lead: The testosterone-boosting diet is a food-based approach in which people emphasise eggs, oysters, red meat and similar foods, marketed or believed to raise testosterone. It is discussed in looksmaxxing and fitness circles as a way to support muscularity, masculine features and energy.

Wikipedia's testosterone article reports that deficiencies of vitamin A and zinc may lower testosterone, that vitamin D intakes of roughly 400 to 1000 IU per day were associated with higher levels, and that evidence on dietary fat is limited, with low-fat diets possibly lowering total and free testosterone.[1] It also states that zinc supplementation beyond sufficiency has no effect on serum testosterone.[1] No source reviewed shows that a foods-only diet raises testosterone in men who are not deficient.
infobox: Eggs, oysters, beef and other red meat

paras: Proponents promote foods rich in zinc, fat, cholesterol and protein. Oysters are the richest dietary zinc source, and beef, pork and lamb are also good sources.[2]

Wikipedia reports that zinc is required for testosterone production and that deficiency can reduce circulating testosterone and cause hypogonadism, while over-supplementation has no effect on serum testosterone.[1][2] Testosterone also declines with age, and weight loss may raise it because fat tissue contains aromatase.[1]

The oyster article says two oysters supply the daily reference intake of zinc and describes oysters' traditional aphrodisiac reputation, including a research team reporting amino acids linked to sex hormone increases.[3]
No studies found. The cited material describes nutrient-level and deficiency research (zinc, vitamin D, fat intake) rather than trials of an eggs, oysters and red meat diet as such.[1][2]
Raw oysters can carry Vibrio bacteria that are dangerous to immunocompromised people.[3]

card.summary: Eggs, oysters and beef as a T booster: nutrient deficiencies matter, but no trial shows the diet lifts testosterone in men who are already replete.
card.note: Zinc supplements above sufficiency do not raise testosterone, per Wikipedia.

quick.overview:
This is the belief that eating eggs, oysters and red meat raises testosterone. Zinc, vitamin D and dietary fat are the nutrients usually invoked.

Deficiency in some nutrients lowers testosterone, but the sources describe no trial of this specific diet.
quick.mechanism: Zinc is needed for testosterone production, and low-fat diets may lower levels. Food supplies these nutrients; effects beyond correcting a shortfall are not shown.
quick.risks: Raw shellfish carries bacterial food-safety risks. No specific harms of the diet itself are described in the sources.
